newsitem.title: USA: U.S. group urges tougher truck, driver restriction.
newsitem.headline: U.S. group urges tougher truck, driver restriction.

text.p: A highway safety group Monday urged Congress to keep weight and size limits on trucks and tighten rules on how long truck drivers work.

"The public wants safer roads and that means safer trucks," Joan Claybrook, chairwoman of Citizens for Reliable and Safe Highways (CRASH), told a news conference. Her group said 4,903 people were killed in U.S. accidents involving trucks in 1995, including 749 truck drivers. The figures were down from the previous three years.
California had the most truck-related deaths, 433, followed by Texas with 381, Florida with 290, Ohio with 218 and Georgia with 201.

CRASH called for a continuation of the freeze on combination vehicles such as triple trailer trucks, which has been in effect since 1991. Claybrook said longer trucks caused problems on highways, especially when using on and off ramps.

Claybrook, who was highway traffic safety administrator in the Transportation Department from 1977-81, said current rules that allow truck drivers to work 60 hours in a seven-day period were too high and often led to driver fatigue. But she did not recommend a specific change.

The rules say drivers can work no more than 10 hours straight and then must take an eight-hour break. The Transportation Department will hold public meetings around the country in March to hear comments from truck drivers and others on whether the limits should be changed.
The American Trucking Association, which represents major truck companies, challenged CRASH's findings, saying truck safety was improving.
"Since 1979, truck-related fatalities have decreased 27 percent. In fact, 1995 (latest available reports) was trucking's safest year on record," the association said.
"The vast majority of trucks on the road are in safe condition and are contiually improving," it added.
ATA said CRASH received some of its funds from the Association of American Railroads, which it said had a financial interest in distorting the trucking industry's safety record.
